slides.title: Direct Sign-In lifecycle
slides.subtitle: Take the callback once, exchange the code, keep the tokens in the host
slides.notes: This example picks up where the boundary example stopped: the user has approved on the company's page. The host now has to turn the browser callback into tokens, once, and without widening access.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.statement: Sign-in names **no Session**. Partial consent is a **result**, not an error.
slides.notes: Sign-in is plain OAuth. A Session is signed in on each request that carries the access token, so the conversation carries on in the Session it already has. And if the user grants less than was asked, the host reports it plainly instead of quietly asking for more.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph USR["User, trusted browser"] direction TB B["Browser
orders:read granted"] end subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB R[("Reactor state store")] -- "pending state, once" --> H["PAP host"] H -- "sign" --> P["Reactor signer"] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB A["Authorization server"] end USR -- "code, state, issuer" --> HOST HOST -- "exchange, client assertion" --> CO HOST -. "status, scopes, reference" .-> M
slides.caption: The callback comes in, the exchange goes out; the model gets a status and a reference.
slides.notes: Start with the user, who approves orders:read and declines orders:return. The company redirects the browser to the host's registered HTTPS callback, carrying a code, the state and the issuer. In the host, the PAP host takes the pending state out of the Reactor state store, once, and asks the signer for a fresh client assertion. It then exchanges the code with the company's authorization server. Off to the side, the model: it learns that the user is signed in, which scopes were granted and which are missing, and a refresh token reference, never a token.

slides.title: From callback to checks

items.title: Callback
items.detail: Code, state and issuer reach the host

slides.notes: The callback carries a code, the state and the issuer. The host takes the pending request out of the store in one atomic step, getting back the verifier, then checks the redirect, state, issuer and expiry.

slides.title: The exchange

items.title: Tokens
items.detail: A Bearer access token and a refresh token

slides.notes: The host exchanges the code with the PKCE verifier and a fresh client assertion. The answer is plain OAuth: a Bearer access token, with orders:read, and a refresh token. This company lists no DPoP algorithm, so no proof goes. Nothing on the wire names a Session; the next request that carries the access token signs its Session in.

slides.title: What gets validated
items: Redirect location, issuer, state and expiry
Content type, response size and token type
No Session named: one sign-in can serve several Sessions
Scopes: never more than requested; missing ones reported
slides.notes: Everything the company sends back is checked. If the company returns a scope the user was never asked for, the host rejects it. Scopes that are missing are reported, so the application can degrade or explain.

slides.title: A replayed callback
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR C1["Callback"] --> Q{"Pending state
in the store?"} C2["Same callback again"] --> Q Q -- "no" --> X["Rejected"] Q -- "yes" --> T["Take it atomically
store now empty"] T --> V["Verify and exchange"] V -- "succeeds" --> S["Signed in"] V -- "fails" --> F["Failed"]
slides.caption: State is consumed before the exchange, so whatever happens next, a second callback finds nothing.
slides.notes: Follow the first callback: the pending state is in the store, so the host takes it out in one atomic step, and only then verifies and exchanges. Whether the exchange then succeeds or fails, the store is already empty. Now follow the same callback submitted again, from the bottom left: it finds no pending state and is rejected. The example does exactly this and reports the rejection.

slides.title: What stays where

right.heading: What the user and model see

slides.notes: The refresh token goes into the host's token store before complete returns; the result carries only a reference. No token reaches URLs, logs, analytics, React state or a model transcript.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples grant only orders:read, then replay the callback
slides.notes: Both examples ask for read and return access, get read only, and show the replayed callback being rejected. The Direct Sign-In guide covers the production setup.
